title: Porter: value = outcomes per dollar spent

summary: Michael Porter, a Harvard Business School strategy professor, argues that the overarching goal of health care delivery should be value for patients, defined as the health outcomes achieved relative to the money spent to achieve them. In this framing, value is measured around the patient and the full cycle of care for a medical condition, not around individual services, departments or visits. Cost reduction without regard to outcomes is not value improvement, and neither is quality improvement measured only by process compliance. Porter's 2010 NEJM essay laid out how outcomes and costs should both be measured per patient over the care cycle, which became the conceptual foundation for later work on integrated practice units, outcome standard sets (ICHOM) and time-driven activity-based costing. For practitioners in value-based care, the practical implication is that any program claim of 'value' needs both a credible outcome measure and a credible cost measure for the same defined population and condition.

title: Porter & Teisberg: zero-sum vs positive-sum competition

summary: Michael Porter and Elizabeth Teisberg first sketched their critique in a 2004 Harvard Business Review article and expanded it in the 2006 book Redefining Health Care (Harvard Business School Press). Their diagnosis is that US health care competition happens at the wrong level: payers, plans and providers compete to shift costs, restrict access and capture bargaining power, which divides value rather than creating it. They call this zero-sum competition. Their prescription is positive-sum, value-based competition on results, occurring at the level of preventing, diagnosing and treating specific medical conditions, supported by widely available condition-level outcome and price information and by providers that specialize in conditions where they can excel. The book is the origin of the later 'value agenda' and the outcome-per-dollar definition of value. For VBC practitioners, it frames why contracting on total cost alone, without condition-level outcome transparency, can still be zero-sum.

summary: In his 2010 NEJM essay 'What Is Value in Health Care?', Porter proposed that outcomes for any medical condition be organized in a three-tier hierarchy. Tier 1 is health status achieved or retained (survival; degree of health or recovery). Tier 2 is the process of recovery (time to recovery and return to normal activities; disutility of the care process). Tier 3 is the sustainability of health (sustainability of recovery; long-term consequences of therapy). Each tier has two levels, giving six levels in total. The hierarchy was intended to push measurement beyond mortality and process compliance toward the results that patients experience, and it underlies ICHOM's condition-specific standard sets. A 2021 systematic review found that few published value-based initiatives measured outcomes at all six levels, illustrating the gap between the framework and practice. Practitioners can use the tiers as a checklist when designing outcome dashboards for a population or service line.

The authors present IPUs as the core and the other components as enablers; they argue the agenda is a strategy for providers rather than a policy mandate. Later peer-reviewed reviews describe the six elements the same way and report that few organizations have implemented all of them. For VBC practitioners, the agenda is a useful checklist for whether a contract strategy is supported by matching care-delivery, measurement and data capabilities.

summary: An integrated practice unit is Porter's term for a care team organized around a medical condition or a defined patient segment (for example, primary care for a population with similar needs) rather than around a specialty or a type of service. The IPU brings together the clinicians and support services needed over the full care cycle, takes responsibility for that cycle, and measures its own outcomes and costs. In the 2013 Porter and Lee value agenda the IPU is the first and central component; bundled payments, outcome and cost measurement, system integration and IT are meant to reinforce it. Published implementations include condition-based units such as joint replacement, cancer and psoriasis clinics that use time-driven activity-based costing to cost the full cycle. For VBC practitioners managing populations, the IPU idea translates into designing care teams for high-need segments (for example frail elderly, advanced CKD, heart failure) and measuring segment-level outcomes rather than practice-level averages.

title: Time-driven activity-based costing (Kaplan & Porter, HBR 2011)

summary: Robert Kaplan and Michael Porter argued in the September 2011 Harvard Business Review article 'How to Solve the Cost Crisis in Health Care' that providers measure costs the wrong way: charges and departmental allocations do not show what it actually costs to treat a patient's condition. They proposed time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC), which maps each step of a patient's care cycle, estimates the time each clinician or resource spends, and multiplies that time by the capacity cost rate of the resource. The result is a patient-level cost for the full cycle that can be paired with outcomes to measure value, used to redesign processes, and used to set bundled prices. A 2025 systematic review found TDABC applied mostly in cancer and diabetes care, with 32 eligible studies, and reported that it helped identify resource waste where traditional cost accounting could not. For VBC organizations, TDABC is a tool for understanding the internal cost of care programs and episodes rather than relying on claims-paid amounts.

summary: The International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement (ICHOM) is a nonprofit founded in 2012 by Michael Porter of Harvard Business School, Stefan Larsson of Boston Consulting Group and Martin Ingvar of the Karolinska Institute. It convenes clinicians, researchers and patients to define condition-specific sets of outcome measures, including patient-reported outcomes and the case-mix variables needed to compare results fairly, and promotes their adoption worldwide. ICHOM reports having published 48 sets. Porter, Larsson and Lee argued in NEJM in 2016 that standardized outcome measurement is a prerequisite for value-based competition and for comparing providers. For VBC analytics, ICHOM sets are a ready-made source of outcome definitions when a program needs measures beyond claims-based utilization and HEDIS-style process measures.

summary: Donald Berwick, Thomas Nolan and John Whittington of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement argued in Health Affairs in 2008 that the US health system needs to pursue three aims at the same time: better experience of care, better health of populations, and lower per capita cost. Pursuing any one alone tends to undermine the others; for example, cost cutting without attention to population health or patient experience. The Triple Aim became a widely used organizing frame for accountable care, population health management and CMS strategy. The paper also specifies preconditions: an identified, enrolled population, a commitment to serve all of its members, and an 'integrator' organization that accepts responsibility for all three aims for that population. For VBC organizations, the Triple Aim is a reminder that savings claims should be paired with population health and experience measures for the same attributed population.

summary: Beyond naming the three aims, Berwick, Nolan and Whittington described what it takes to pursue them. Preconditions are an identified population, a commitment to universality for its members, and an integrator: an organization that accepts responsibility for all three aims for that population. They list at least five integrator functions: partnership with individuals and families, redesign of primary care, population health management, financial management, and macro-system integration. This concept anticipated the accountable care organization, in which a provider-led entity takes accountability for cost and quality for an attributed population. For practitioners, the integrator functions map onto practical ACO capabilities: patient engagement, primary care transformation, risk stratification and care management, financial and contract management, and coordination with hospitals, post-acute and community services.

summary: Thomas Bodenheimer and Christine Sinsky proposed in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2014 that the Triple Aim be extended to a Quadruple Aim by adding a fourth goal: improving the work life of health care providers, including clinicians and staff. Their reasoning is that widespread burnout and dissatisfaction among the workforce are associated with lower patient satisfaction and worse outcomes and may raise costs, so neglecting the workforce undermines the other three aims. The Quadruple Aim is now commonly cited in primary care transformation and value-based care programs. Practically, it argues that care management, documentation, quality reporting and risk-coding workflows introduced under VBC contracts should be designed to reduce, not add to, clinician burden, and that workforce measures belong on the same scorecard as cost, quality and experience.

This definition is widely cited and emphasizes distribution (equity) as well as averages. In VBC usage, 'population health management' usually means something narrower: managing the care and cost of an attributed panel. summary: Atul Gawande's January 2011 New Yorker article 'The Hot Spotters' described efforts, including the work of Camden, New Jersey physician Jeffrey Brenner (later founder of the Camden Coalition), to identify the small group of patients who account for a large share of costs and give them intensive, coordinated medical and social support. The article asked whether lowering costs could be achieved by giving the neediest patients better care, and it helped make 'hotspotting' and superutilizer programs a national policy idea. The Camden Coalition later took part in a randomized trial: Finkelstein and colleagues (NEJM 2020) found its care-transition program did not reduce 180-day readmissions versus usual care, and that a pre-post comparison would have wrongly suggested a large effect. For practitioners, the story is a case study in why high-cost cohort programs need randomized or well-controlled evaluation because extreme utilization tends to fall on its own.

title: Early MSSP performance (McWilliams et al., NEJM 2016)

summary: McWilliams and colleagues used a difference-in-differences design on Medicare claims from 2009 to 2013 to compare beneficiaries served by the 220 ACOs that entered the Medicare Shared Savings Program in 2012 or 2013 with beneficiaries of non-ACO providers in the same areas. Pre-contract spending trends were similar. In 2013, the 2012 entrants showed a differential spending change of -$144 per beneficiary (about 1.4% savings, P=0.02), whereas 2013 entrants showed essentially no change (-$3, P=0.96). Savings were consistently larger in independent primary care groups than in hospital-integrated groups, and quality measures improved on some dimensions and were unchanged on others. The study established the modest-savings baseline for the MSSP literature. Limitations include its observational design and short follow-up, and that early entrants may have been unusually motivated. For practitioners, it signals that savings in shared-savings contracts are small in year one and vary by organizational type.

title: MSSP after 3 years: physician-group vs hospital-integrated ACOs (NEJM 2018)
questions: Do physician-led ACOs save more than hospital ACOs?

summary: Using fee-for-service Medicare claims from 2009 to 2015, McWilliams and colleagues estimated difference-in-differences changes in spending for MSSP ACO patients versus local non-participants, separately for physician-group and hospital-integrated ACOs entering in 2012, 2013 or 2014. Savings in physician-group ACOs grew with tenure: by 2015 the differential change was -$474 per patient (-4.9%) for 2012 entrants, -$342 (-3.5%) for 2013 entrants and -$156 (-1.6%) for 2014 entrants. Hospital-integrated ACOs showed -$169, -$18 and +$88 respectively, significantly smaller. Physician-group savings represented net savings to Medicare of $256.4 million in 2015 after bonuses, while hospital-integrated reductions were offset by bonus payments. The study is observational and cannot fully exclude selection. The practical lesson is that organizations without hospital revenue at stake have stronger incentives to reduce hospital use, and that ACO savings take years to mature.

The usual explanation is incentives: reducing admissions cuts hospital revenue. Caveats: these are observational comparisons, organization types self-select, and benchmark-based CMS figures are not causal estimates.

summary: Markovitz, Ryan and colleagues studied a 20% sample of fee-for-service Medicare (2008-2014, about 97 million beneficiary-quarters). In conventional adjusted longitudinal models, the MSSP was associated with spending reductions of -$118 per beneficiary-quarter and better quality. But when they used the share of nearby clinicians in the MSSP as an instrumental variable to address nonrandom participation, the effect disappeared (+$5 per beneficiary-quarter, CI -$51 to $62). A falsification test supported their concern: the conventional model implausibly showed the MSSP reducing hip fracture hospitalizations, while the IV model did not. High-cost clinicians (99th percentile) had a 30.4% chance of exiting versus 13.8% for median-cost clinicians, suggesting exits of costly clinicians and panels could create apparent savings. The study is observational and instrument validity is debated. Practitioners should expect evaluators to scrutinize roster changes and panel turnover when attributing savings.

summary: Ryan and Markovitz combined publicly reported MSSP bonus payments for performance years 2013-2021 with gross spending effects taken from two earlier academic evaluations to estimate the program's net budget impact. Because MSSP lowers fee-for-service spending, it also lowers Medicare Advantage benchmarks; counting that spillover ($4.48-$4.92 billion), the program was associated with overall CMS savings of $3.06-$4.34 billion, about 0.075% of combined spending. The paper was retracted and replaced after a calculation error regarding how MSSP incentive payments enter MA benchmark rates was identified. Results depend heavily on which gross-savings estimates are used; they rely on early-cohort estimates. Practitioners should distinguish benchmark-based savings from causal net savings when citing MSSP results.

summary: Value-based payment results are reported in several incompatible ways. title: Maryland Total Cost of Care model evaluation, 2019-2022
questions: Is the Maryland Total Cost of Care model saving money?
What were the results of Maryland's TCOC model?
How do hospital global budgets affect Medicare spending?
summary: Maryland's Total Cost of Care model (2019-2026) continues all-payer hospital global budgets begun under the 2014-2018 All-Payer Model and adds a primary care program (508 practices reaching about half of Medicare beneficiaries), episode programs and grant funding. CMS's findings-at-a-glance for the evaluation of the first four years reports cumulative effects since 2014 during 2019-2022 of -2.1% total Medicare spending, -6.1% hospital spending, +3.1% non-hospital spending, -16.2% hospital admissions, -5.9% outpatient ED visits and -16.8% preventable admissions, and $689 million in net savings to Medicare over the model's first three years after non-claims payments. The evaluators note that since 2019 effects on service use and quality have been sustained but not increased, while total spending effects have shrunk as non-hospital spending rose. Effects are measured against a comparison group and reflect all changes since 2014. Practitioners should note that global budgets can shift spending outside the hospital.

title: Oncology Care Model: modest savings, net loss (Brooks et al., JAMA 2026)
questions: Did the Oncology Care Model save money?
What were the final OCM results?
Does episode-based oncology payment reduce spending?
summary: The Oncology Care Model (2016-2022) paid participating oncology practices a monthly enhanced services payment plus performance-based payments tied to 6-month chemotherapy episodes. Brooks, Keating and colleagues compared episodes at 202 OCM practices (about 740,000 beneficiaries, 1.75 million episodes) with 534 propensity-matched comparison practices using difference-in-differences. OCM was associated with a $616 reduction in total episode payments (90% CI -$912 to -$321), growing to -$1,282 in the final period, with significant reductions in Part A and Part B but not Part D. There were no significant differences in hospitalizations, ED visits or quality. After counting enhanced services and performance-based payments, OCM produced an estimated net loss to Medicare of $639 million over six years. An earlier evaluation abstract found a small relative reduction in end-of-life hospitalizations without change in hospice use. Practitioners should expect specialty episode models to need lower add-on payments to break even.

title: Comprehensive ESRD Care (ESCO) model evaluation, years 1-4
questions: Did kidney care ACOs (ESCOs) save money?
What did the Comprehensive ESRD Care evaluation find?
Do specialty ACOs for dialysis patients work?
summary: The Comprehensive ESRD Care model, launched in October 2015, let dialysis facilities and nephrologists form ESRD Seamless Care Organizations (ESCOs), specialty ACOs accountable for total Part A and B spending and quality for aligned dialysis patients. By PY4, 37 ESCOs had participated, including 1,172 dialysis facilities (16% of US facilities) and about 63,640 beneficiaries. CMS's evaluation summary for years 1-4 reports that the model reduced Medicare spending by $151 million (1.3% relative to the pre-model period), driven mainly by first-wave ESCOs, with 3% fewer hospitalizations, 6% fewer hospitalizations for ESRD complications, 5% lower catheter use and 8% better phosphate-binder adherence. After shared savings payments to ESCOs, however, Medicare had aggregate net losses of $46 million. A separate analysis found ESCO markets were larger and higher-spending than non-ESCO markets. CEC was followed by the Kidney Care Choices model, whose results are not covered here.

title: Medicare Advantage vs traditional Medicare spending and utilization (Curto et al., 2019)
questions: Do Medicare Advantage plans spend less than traditional Medicare?
Is MA spending lower because of prices or utilization?
How profitable are Medicare Advantage insurers?
summary: Curto, Einav, Finkelstein, Levin and Bhattacharya compared health care spending in Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare using newly available claims from MA insurers. Insurer revenues were about 30% higher than their health care spending. After adjusting for enrollee mix, health care spending per enrollee was 9% to 30% lower in MA than in traditional Medicare, depending on how comparable enrollees were defined. The difference came mainly from lower utilization rather than lower prices, with similar reductions in services considered high-value and low-value, consistent with plans steering patients to cheaper settings and using utilization management. The study relies on claims from a subset of insurers and on assumptions to construct comparable populations, and it does not establish health outcome effects. For VBC practitioners, it shows MA plans can deliver care with lower resource use, but that lower spending is not the same as lower Medicare payments to plans.

title: Upcoding in Medicare Advantage (Geruso & Layton, JPE 2020)
questions: How much higher are Medicare Advantage risk scores?
What is coding intensity in Medicare Advantage?
Does vertical integration increase coding?
summary: Geruso and Layton studied how diagnosis-based risk adjustment creates incentives for insurers to 'upcode', i.e., record more diagnoses to raise risk-adjusted payments. Using variation in Medicare Advantage enrollment, they estimate that the same people generate 6% to 16% higher risk scores in private Medicare plans than they would in fee-for-service Medicare, where diagnoses do not affect most provider payments. Their estimates imply billions of dollars in excess public spending and distortions to plan and consumer behavior. Coding intensity rises with vertical integration between insurers and providers, pointing to a principal-agent problem in which insurers want providers to code more intensively. The study identifies coding differences, not whether additional codes are clinically accurate. For VBC organizations taking MA or ACO risk, it explains why regulators apply coding-intensity adjustments and audits, and why risk-score growth is a central policy concern.

title: MedPAC 2025: MA payments 20% above FFS, driven by selection and coding
questions: How much more does Medicare pay for Medicare Advantage enrollees?
What does MedPAC say about MA coding intensity and favorable selection?
How large is Medicare Advantage in 2024?
summary: MedPAC's March 2025 status report on Medicare Advantage states that in 2024 MA enrolled about 33.6 million beneficiaries (54% of those with Parts A and B), offered 5,678 plan options from 175 organizations, and was paid an estimated $494 billion excluding drug coverage. MedPAC estimates that in 2025 Medicare will spend 20% more for MA enrollees than if they were in fee-for-service Medicare, about $84 billion, and identifies favorable selection (enrollees with lower actual spending than their risk scores predict) and coding intensity (more diagnoses recorded in MA) as the two largest drivers. Higher MA payments also raise Part B premiums for all beneficiaries, about $13 billion in 2025. The extra payments fund rebates and supplemental benefits, but MedPAC notes there is little reliable information on their use or value. The report recommends reforms to payment levels, the quality bonus program and benchmarks. These are MedPAC projections built on its own selection and coding estimates, not audited amounts.

title: Medicaid managed care mandates did not reduce spending (Duggan & Hayford 2013)
questions: Does Medicaid managed care save money?
Did moving Medicaid to managed care lower costs?
What is the evidence on Medicaid MCOs and spending?
summary: Between 1991 and 2009 the share of Medicaid recipients in HMOs and other managed care rose from 11% to 71%, largely because states and localities mandated enrollment. Duggan and Hayford used the timing of these state and local mandates together with CMS data on state Medicaid expenditures to estimate the effect of shifting enrollees from fee-for-service into managed care. On average, the shift did not reduce Medicaid spending; if anything it increased spending, particularly for risk-based HMOs. Effects varied substantially across states and depended on how generous the state's baseline fee-for-service provider payment rates were: in states that already paid providers very little, managed care plans had less room to save. The study measures spending, not quality or access, and predates the expansion era. For practitioners, it cautions that capitation alone does not guarantee savings when the fee-for-service baseline is already low-priced.

title: CBO 2023: CMMI increased federal spending in its first decade
questions: Has the CMS Innovation Center saved money?
What did CBO conclude about CMMI?
How many CMMI models produced savings?
summary: In September 2023 the Congressional Budget Office reviewed published evaluations of 49 models launched in CMMI's first decade and concluded that the center's activities increased net federal spending by about $5.4 billion over 2011-2020, rather than producing the savings CBO originally projected in 2010. CBO estimated that CMMI spent about $7.9 billion to operate models, while the models reduced spending on health benefits by about $2.6 billion. CBO also projected that CMMI would increase net spending by about $1.3 billion over 2021-2030. A 2026 GAO report notes that of 70 models tested as of January 2025, CMS certified four for expansion based on net savings: Pioneer ACO, the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program, prior authorization for repetitive non-emergent ambulance transport, and Home Health Value-Based Purchasing. GAO also highlights voluntary participation, incentive payments and participant attrition (0% to 78% across 18 completed models) as obstacles to demonstrating savings.

title: GAO 2026: why voluntary CMMI models struggle to show savings
questions: Why don't more CMMI models save money?
What did GAO find about the CMS Innovation Center in 2026?
Which CMMI models were expanded nationally?
summary: GAO's March 2026 report on the CMS Innovation Center reviewed obligations and model testing progress through January 2025. Of 70 models tested, CMS had certified four for expansion because they achieved net savings during testing: the Pioneer ACO model ($384 million in Medicare savings in its first two years), the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program ($2,650 per beneficiary in the first 15 months), the Repetitive Scheduled Non-Emergent Ambulance Transport prior authorization model ($1 billion over five years) and Home Health Value-Based Purchasing ($949 million, 2016-2020). GAO describes features of voluntary models that make savings harder to demonstrate, including incentive payments to participants, selection bias in who joins, and participant attrition, which ranged from zero to 78% across 18 completed models. For VBC practitioners, these findings explain CMS's recent emphasis on mandatory models, smaller incentive payments and tighter benchmarks.

title: Systematic review of ACO effects across payers (Kaufman et al., 2019)
questions: What does the research say about ACOs overall?
Do ACOs reduce hospital use?
Is there a systematic review of accountable care organizations?
summary: Kaufman and colleagues systematically reviewed 42 studies of accountable care organization contracts with Medicare (24 studies), Medicaid (5), commercial insurers (11) and all payers (2), assessing the quality of evidence on health service use, processes of care and outcomes. The most consistent associations across payer types were reduced inpatient use, reduced emergency department visits, and improved preventive care and chronic disease management measures. The seven studies of patient experience or clinical outcomes found no evidence that ACOs worsen care. The review predates longer-term MSSP, NGACO and REACH evaluations and does not synthesize net spending after bonus payments; most included studies are observational with voluntary participation. For practitioners, it supports the claim that ACOs modestly reduce acute care use without harming quality, but not, on its own, claims of large net savings.
